title: The communion of saints
hook: the living and the dead are one family; traditions differ on praying with the saints

segments.voice: Yesterday, catholic with a small c: according to the whole. Your line was universal. Who did you let into your circle? Day three hundred seven.

The last lap of a long race. Your legs are burning. Your lungs are on fire. You're thinking about stopping. And then you look up at the stands, and they're full. Packed, row on row, all the way up. And every single person in those seats has run this race before you. They know exactly how it feels. Some of them stumbled. Some of them finished crawling. And they're all on their feet, cheering for you. That's the picture the letter to the Hebrews paints, right after a long chapter listing the heroes of faith: Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and others the writer says he hasn't time to name. Today's word is the line of the creed that says those stands are real.
screen: `THE LAST LAP.` → `THE STANDS ARE FULL.` → `EVERYONE THERE RAN IT BEFORE YOU.`

segments.voice: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us." That's Hebrews, chapter twelve. The creed puts it in four words: the communion of saints. Start with saints. In the New Testament, saints doesn't mean a few famous holy people with halos. Paul writes to whole churches, ordinary, squabbling congregations, and calls every one of them saints: holy ones, set apart for God. And communion means sharing, fellowship, having in common. So the communion of saints is the whole family of God's people sharing one life: on earth now, and those who have died in Christ. Death doesn't end the family. Here's a scholar's detail: in Latin, communio sanctorum can also mean a sharing in holy things, like the sacraments. Some readers think the line meant both. Churches differ on what this means in practice, and they say so plainly. Catholic and Orthodox Christians ask the saints, especially Mary, to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend to pray for you, and they keep feast days for them. In much Protestant practice, the saints are honored as examples and given thanks for, but prayer goes to God alone, because that's how those churches read scripture. Anglicans and Lutherans often keep saints' days while praying in different ways. What they share is the stadium: nobody runs alone, and the ones who went before are not lost. Hebrews pictures them all around the track.
screen: `SAINTS: ALL GOD'S HOLY ONES.` · `COMMUNION: SHARING ONE LIFE.` · `HOLY PEOPLE, OR HOLY THINGS?` · `CHURCHES DIFFER ON PRAYING WITH THEM.` · then, large: `SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trace the chain. Settle, and breathe. Think of one good thing you carry: a way of praying, a kindness, a stubborn honesty. Who handed it to you? A grandmother, a teacher, a coach. Then ask: who handed it to them? Follow the chain back, name by name, until the names run out. Picture them in the stands, on their feet. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for them, or ask them to pray for you, as your tradition does. If you don't, just let the chain stand behind you. The bell holds the time.
Communio sanctorum. The creed's Latin words for the whole family of God's people, living and dead, sharing one life.
Your line: a great cloud of witnesses. Today, when you're tired or ready to quit, remember who's in the stands, and keep going one more step. Day three hundred seven.

howItsDone: Western churches keep All Saints' Day on November 1, and some read aloud the names of members who died that year; Orthodox Christians keep All Saints on the Sunday after Pentecost. Catholic and Orthodox Christians also ask the saints for their prayers, while Protestants generally honor them as examples.

options: a great cloud of witnesses who ran the race before you.
fork.reveal: Hebrews 12 pictures the faithful who went before as a great cloud of witnesses, surrounding those still running.

original.note: Latin: the communion of saints, or of holy things. The creed's words.

trapdoor: what you thought: saints are a few perfect people with halos.
what it means: all God's people, living and dead, one family sharing one life. churches differ on praying with them.
what a scholar hears: sanctorum can be masculine or neuter: holy ones, or holy things. the line may have meant both.
